meta.title: The Drawer: who keeps your gift card money?
meta.description: Maya's grandma gave her a $50 gift card. It sat in a kitchen drawer for four years. So who had that fifty dollars all that time? The Catch, Case 001.

source.name: Bankrate gift card survey 2024 (YouGov, 2,373 US adults)
Credit CARD Act 2009, 12 CFR 1005.20; Cal. Civ. Code 1749.5

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: This is fifty dollars.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Four years in a kitchen drawer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: So who's had it all this time?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Not Maya. Not her grandma.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Birthday card. Little heart on the envelope.

beats.speaker: maya
beats.line: I was saving it for something special.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Shh. Follow the money.

params.caption: US adults with an unused gift card

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Maya's not careless. She's normal.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: More than four in ten American adults have a gift card they haven't used.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: The average? $244 each.
beats.spoken: The average? Two hundred and forty-four dollars each.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Add it up and it's about $27 billion.
beats.spoken: Add it up and it's about twenty-seven billion dollars.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: In drawers, wallets, old phone apps.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Doing a job. Just not for us.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Then for who?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: When Maya's grandma bought that card, the store got fifty dollars. Cash. That day.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: But the store didn't sell anything.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: No sweater left the shelf. No book. Nothing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: So accountants don't call it a sale. They call it a debt.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: The store owes whoever holds the card fifty dollars of stuff.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: It's an IOU. And IOUs have a funny feature.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Until you show up, the money just sits with the store.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: No interest. No rent. No questions.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Free money. Until you come back.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Now picture that at the size of a coffee chain.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Starbucks customers load money onto cards and the app before they order.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Auto-reload, ten here, twenty-five there.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: In early 2024, that pile was about $2.2 billion.
beats.spoken: In early twenty twenty-four, that pile was about two point two billion dollars.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Money that's paid, but not yet spent.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: If you lent a bank two billion dollars, it would pay you interest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Lend it to a coffee shop and you get… coffee. Later. Maybe.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: That's why people joke that Starbucks is a bank that sells coffee.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: It isn't a bank. But for that money, it gets the best part of being one.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Cheap money. Very cheap.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: But that's not the strange part.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: The strange part is the money nobody ever comes back for.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Every year, some balances never get spent.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: $3.17 left on a card. A card lost in a move.
beats.spoken: Three dollars and seventeen cents left on a card. A card lost in a move.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Retailers have a word for that money: breakage.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: They look at years of history and estimate how much you'll never use.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Then they count it as revenue.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: In one year, Starbucks booked about $188 million of it.
beats.spoken: In one year, Starbucks booked about a hundred and eighty-eight million dollars of it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: That's coffee nobody drank.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Coffee. Nobody. Drank.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: And why do we forget? Because a gift card doesn't feel like money.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: It feels like a gift. And gifts get saved.

beats.speaker: maya
beats.line: For something special.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Something special is how it ends up in a drawer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: So here's the catch.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: A gift card is two gifts.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: One to the person you give it to.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: And one to the store. A free loan.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: And if life gets busy, it never has to be paid back.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Case closed?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Not yet. Because this time, the rules are on Maya's side.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Under US federal rules, most store gift cards can't expire within 5 years.
beats.spoken: Under US federal rules, most store gift cards can't expire within five years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Five years from when the money was loaded. Maya's four-year-old card? Still good.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: And no inactivity fees until a card's gone a full year unused.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Some states go further.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: In California, under $15 left? You can ask for cash.
beats.spoken: In California, under fifteen dollars left? You can ask for cash.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: So, tonight. Three things.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Open the drawer. Photograph every card and write down the balance.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Spend the smallest ones first. Those are the ones you'll lose.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: And if you're giving one, give it for a place they already go. Every week.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Maya did one more thing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Her grandma always told her to read one book. She never had.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Fifty dollars. Four years late.

beats.speaker: maya
beats.line: It still counts.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: Every gift card has a clock on it. And it's not the expiry date.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.line: It's you, forgetting.

beats.speaker: nickel
beats.line: Check your drawer.
